main.title:
Product Designer
with a Frontend Development Background
main.description: I design interfaces and understand how they are built

about.title: ABOUT
about.text1: I have 5 years of commercial experience as a Frontend Developer in fintech, including 2 years combining development with product design. I designed mobile and web applications for banks and built a modular UI architecture with configurable interface parameters for a no-code platform from scratch. Over time, I realized that what fascinated me most was not writing code, but understanding how an interface should work and why.
about.text2: I transitioned into Product Design, bringing with me a strong understanding of technical constraints, component-based thinking, and a systems-oriented approach. My designs are realistic because I know exactly how they will be built.
about.text3: Designed 10+ landing pages for educational projects (Spanish and English language courses) and the event industry (wedding invitations). Worked directly with clients without formal briefs, defining page goals, user needs, and the visual direction for each project independently.
about.text4: Contributed to the company's internal design system by implementing UI controls, components, and their states while collaborating with designers on technical constraints. Defined reusable design tokens adopted across multiple applications, reducing development time for new screens and improving visual consistency between products.
about.text5: Built reusable UI modules for a page and form builder, designing flexible components that became tools for other designers, as users of the no-code platform assembled their own interfaces from them. Conducted design reviews, helping identify potential implementation issues before features reached production.

1.title: Image Generation
1.text: A cross-platform tool for generating images that can be used to create and share QR code links.

2.title: Bank Details Input Widget
2.text: A reusable input component for bank cards and account numbers with real-time BIN detection, input masking, and cross-platform validation states.

3.title: Dashboard
3.text: A dashboard designed to present key information in a language learning application.

problem.title: TASK
problem.text: Give users the ability to create and share links to QR codes that could be saved and sent to others.

importance.title: WHY IT MATTERS
importance.text: QR codes often need to be used outside the product: sent to another person, added to a website or document, or saved for later use. However, since this was a no-code platform, the solution needed to integrate with its action system, work across both web and mobile devices, and account for differences in available APIs (for example, printing is available only on the web, while the native system “Share” menu is available only on mobile devices).

desition.title: SOLUTION
desition.text1: I chose to create a separate action instead of using the built-in QR code widget, as this allowed me to solve several tasks at once: the same action could also generate thumbnails for page templates — which was an immediate need at the time. The action is triggered by a specific user event, receives the HTML element ID, and uses the html-to-image library to generate an image file.
desition.text2: This approach made the solution more flexible: the number of buttons and the action type could be configured for each client without additional development.

company.title: ABOUT THE COMPANY
company.text: Nocode.ru is a platform for the digital transformation of large and medium-sized businesses, focused on delivering Enterprise solutions.

problem.title: TASK
problem.text: Design a unified, reusable input component capable of working with cards, bank accounts, and a mixed format. It should display the payment system logo, country flag, and currency code, while validating the input as the user enters data.

importance.title: WHY IT MATTERS
importance.text: Payment forms are one of the most challenging stages of interaction with any fintech product. When entering values into a standard input, users often make mistakes when entering card and account numbers, payment systems are not recognized, and there is no way to validate the entered values.

team.title: MY ROLE
team.role1: Worked as part of a team with an analyst and a QA engineer
team.role2: Designed UX/UI based on the internal design system
team.role4: Conducted design reviews of mockups during solution presentations

desition.title: SOLUTION
desition.text1: I designed and implemented this component as part of the no-code platform. I defined the component states (default, hover, focus, active, disabled, error), described the masking and validation logic for each input mode (card, account, card/account), prepared the designs in Figma, and implemented the frontend for both web and mobile/responsive platforms.
desition.text2: The component was built on top of the existing input field to preserve the ability to place elements on both sides of the field, as standard input fields did not support this pattern.

input.adding: ADDING THE WIDGET TO THE FORM
input.textValidator: During development, I faced a lack of requirements for handling card or account numbers without a predefined mask. To solve this issue, I added validation parameters for minimum and maximum character limits to support formats without predefined masks. For example, in card input mode, the standard range is 13 to 19 characters (according to international standards). However, if a user knows that the transfer is made only to a Visa card, the maximum value can be limited to 16 characters — without requiring a predefined mask.
input.text: The unified reusable component replaced fragmented payment data input fields previously used on the platform. Clients gained the ability to configure it for specific payment systems without requiring custom development.
input.mobile: USING THE WIDGET IN A MOBILE APPLICATION

task.title: TASK
task.text1: Create an English learning dashboard in two themes: light and dark.
task.text2: Practice working with grids, components, and color tokens.

desition.title: SOLUTION
desition.text1: I started with a content audit: identified what information should be displayed on the dashboard — progress in current courses, homework completion status, ranking among friends, and overall learning performance.
desition.text2: Next, I grouped the content into meaningful blocks and prioritized them based on user importance. The performance chart was the most information-dense element (daily progress trends and metric comparisons), so I allocated the largest area to it and placed it in the center — according to the F-pattern layout, this is the first attention zone after the top navigation.
desition.text3: I built the “Homework” and “Friends Score” blocks using the same logic: both display a list of items with a progress bar/value on the right. Since the data structure was identical (list + metric), I made them equal in size and aligned them vertically. This creates visual balance in the lower part of the screen and communicates that both sections have the same level of importance rather than one being primary and the other secondary.
desition.text4: The component was built on top of the existing input field to preserve the ability to place elements on both sides of the field, as standard input components did not support this pattern.
